interactions.label: Camera Translation (tx)
interactions.teaches: Translating the camera laterally causes the projection of the fixed point to shift in the opposite direction on the image plane (parallax).

demo_steps.title: Centered Camera
demo_steps.narration: When the camera is perfectly aligned with point P, the projection falls exactly in the center of the image plane (optical axis).

demo_steps.title: Lateral Translation
demo_steps.narration: Moving the camera to the right causes the point's projection to shift to the left side of the image plane, demonstrating parallax.

plan.geometry_notes: Render completely flat in the XY plane (Z=0 for all geometry). Point P is fixed at world coordinates (0, 4). The baseline track is a faint grey line along Y=0 spanning X from -4 to 4. Camera origin O is at (translationX, 0). The image plane is a solid black line segment of length 3 at Y=1, centered on X=translationX. The optical axis is a dashed line from (translationX, 0) up to (translationX, 4). The projection ray is a red line from P(0, 4) to O(translationX, 0). The projected point p lies at the intersection of the ray and the image plane: world coordinate (translationX - translationX/4, 1). Render points using 2D THREE.CircleGeometry and lines with THREE.Line. Colors: P is dark blue, ray and p are red, camera O and image plane are black.
plan.notes: Ensure no 3D primitives (like spheres or cylinders) are used. The slider should directly update the positions of O, the image plane, the optical axis, the ray, and p. The fixed point P remains stationary.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a horizontal strip in which the same wireframe camera appears five times, evenly spaced across a white field and interleaved with thick red arrows. Each camera is a viewing frustum seen from behind and slightly below: a solid black dot at the bottom marks the projection center, four straight edges rise from it to the corners of a wide rectangle standing for the image plane, and lines cross that rectangle to its lower corners, so the pyramid reads as pointing up and away from the viewer. The five copies match exactly in size and orientation. Red arrows run horizontally along the base of the strip, one before the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, and one trailing off the right edge, every arrowhead pointing right. Because the frusta aim away from the viewer while the arrows travel across the picture, the motion is perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it. The sequence illustrates sideways camera motion parallel to the image plane, as when a scene slides past the side window of a moving car, in which the forward velocity component is zero.
authoredInteractions:
- Animation for sliding the camera sideways parallel to the image plane; the frustum translates across the strip while projected scene points shift laterally, showing motion with zero forward component.
- Slider for lateral displacement; the active camera moves from left to right and image-plane vectors lengthen with the displacement, making the relation between side motion and apparent image shift explicit.
- Toggle between the 3-D path and projected optical flow for near versus far points; the flow view shows larger shifts for nearer points, connecting lateral translation to depth-dependent parallax.
authoredContext:
Consider a camera translating laterally, as shown in
the figure. This will happen if you are looking
through a side window of a car at the scene passing by. In this case,
the forward velocity is zero, $V_Z=0$.

Lateral camera motion parallel to the camera plane.

elements: Five ghosted static camera frustums (light grey wireframes) evenly spaced along a horizontal line
Thick red arrows positioned between the static frustums, pointing right to indicate the translation path
Active moving camera frustum (black wireframe with a solid black dot at its center of projection/pinhole)
Near scene point (green sphere) and far scene point (blue sphere) floating in space in front of the cameras
Dashed projection lines connecting the active camera's pinhole to both scene points
Projected points (smaller green and blue dots) on the active camera's image plane
Optical flow vectors (arrows on the image plane) extending from the points' initial projected positions to their current projected positions

interactions.label: Lateral displacement X
interactions.teaches: Translating the camera parallel to the image plane makes scene points appear to shift laterally in the opposite direction.

interactions.label: Play translation
interactions.teaches: Continuous lateral motion highlights the optical flow field, where all points shift parallel to the motion.

interactions.label: View Mode
interactions.teaches: Switching to the camera's perspective reveals motion parallax: closer points shift much faster across the frame than distant ones.

demo_steps.title: Initial state
demo_steps.narration: The camera starts at the left. In the 3D view, observe the near green point and far blue point in space, and where their projection lines intersect the image plane.

demo_steps.title: Lateral shift
demo_steps.narration: Translate the camera sideways. The projection lines change angle, but the camera's forward distance to the points remains constant.

demo_steps.title: Optical flow
demo_steps.narration: From the camera's perspective, the scene appears to slide leftward. The flow vectors track each point's displacement from the starting frame.

demo_steps.title: Motion parallax
demo_steps.narration: As translation continues, the near green point sweeps across the image plane twice as fast as the far blue point, providing a strong depth cue.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: 5 static ghosted frustums evenly spaced at X = -4, -2, 0, 2, 4. Pinhole at local (0,0,0). Image plane at Z=-2, sized 3x2 (X spans ±1.5, Y spans ±1). Wireframe lines connect the pinhole to the 4 corners. Color: light grey #dddddd. 4 thick red arrows (#ff0000) at Y=-1.2, spanning the horizontal gaps between the static frustums to indicate +X motion. Active camera: Same geometry but black #000000, with a sphere (r=0.15) at the pinhole. Its position Cx is driven by the 'displacement' slider. Near point: green sphere #22aa22 at (0, 0.75, -6). Far point: blue sphere #2222bb at (0, -0.75, -12). Projected points lie on the active camera's image plane at local coordinates x = -Cx*(2/|Pz|), y = Py*(2/|Pz|). Flow vectors are drawn on the image plane from the initial projection at Cx=-4 (green: 1.33, 0.25; blue: 0.67, -0.125) to the current projected coordinates.
interactionPlan.notes: In '3D Path' mode, use the main perspective camera. In 'Camera View' mode, snap the Three.js camera to the active camera's pinhole, pointing down its -Z axis, matching its aspect and FOV to perfectly frame the 3x2 image plane rectangle. Update projection lines, projected points, and flow vectors reactively as the active camera's X position changes.

discrepancies: The sequence of cameras is oriented vertically instead of horizontally.
The camera frustums are rendered as 3D wireframe pyramids instead of the simple 2D rectangle-and-triangle shapes from the source.
The camera pinhole nodes are rendered as 3D spheres instead of flat 2D circles.
The translation arrows are rendered as 3D cylinders and cones instead of flat 2D arrows.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure incorrectly uses 3D primitives and a flawed camera angle that rotates a horizontally-translating 2D diagram into a vertical 3D representation, and it completely lacks the required interactive UI controls.
action_items: Draw the figure purely in the XY plane and use a front-on orthographic camera view so the horizontal layout is preserved.
Replace the 3D wireframes, spheres, and cylindrical arrows with flat 2D lines and shapes to match the simplistic style of the original diagram.
Add a functional HTML UI (like a slider or step buttons) to interactively demonstrate the camera translation, instead of relying on invisible hitboxes.
plan_action_items: Change the modeling approach from a 3D layout to a strictly 2D flat diagram rendered front-on in the XY plane.
